note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting for a diabetes review following a hypoglycaemic episode.
The patient experienced a hypoglycaemic episode last Tuesday after skipping lunch while gardening, presenting with symptoms including sweating, shakiness, and confusion.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused and measured his capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L.
The patient recovered from the hypoglycaemia within 15 minutes after being treated with orange juice and biscuits.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient reports pins and needles in the hands at night, which the relative suspects is carpal tunnel syndrome.
The patient has no visual problems, but his retinal screening is due.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1g twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 mg.
The patient is prescribed Ramipril 5 mg.
The patient's pedal pulses are palpable.
Monofilament sensation is normal in both feet.
A callus is present under the ball of the left first metatarsal head.
The patient's blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kg.
The patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is an increase from the previous level of 58.
The patient's eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide and an HbA1c above target.
The patient has stable CKD stage 3a.
The patient has a low-risk foot with a callus.
The plan is to reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only and stop the teatime dose.
The plan is to start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
The patient will be given a leaflet on sick day rules.
The patient will be referred to a podiatrist for the callus.
The patient will be booked for an eye screening.
The patient will have a review in three months with repeat HbA1c and kidney tests.
The patient should stop empagliflozin if they are unwell, unable to eat or drink, or experiencing vomiting or diarrhoea.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient experienced a funny turn involving being all sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and the patient had just put them out.
The patient had been in the garden all morning and skipped lunch.
The relative found the patient confused and identified the situation as a hypoglycaemia due to her own type 1 diabetes.
The relative gave the patient orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered within about fifteen minutes.
The relative used a meter and the glucose reading was 2.8.
The patient sometimes feels a bit wobbly before tea.
The patient drives to the shops and to his allotment.
The patient is on Metformin 1 gram twice a day.
The patient is on Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day.
The patient takes Gliclazide in the morning and at teatime.
The patient is on Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient's feet have been fine.
The relative has pins and needles in her hands at night, which the clinician suspects is carpal tunnel.
The patient has no problems with his eyesight, but his eye screening is due.
The patient's HbA1c is 62, which is up from 58 last time.
The patient's kidney function, eGFR, is 52, which is about the same as before.
The clinician notes that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypoglycaemia worries the clinician more.
The clinician noted a bit of hard skin and a callus under the ball of the patient's left foot, by the big toe.
The patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84, and his weight is 91 kilos.
The clinician suggested reducing the gliclazide dose to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
The clinician suggested adding empagliflozin 10 milligrams once a day.
The clinician advised stopping empagliflozin if the patient is unwell and not eating or drinking, for example with vomiting or diarrhoea.
The clinician advised the patient to check his blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The clinician advised not to drive if the blood sugar is below five.
The clinician advised the patient to always keep some sugary snacks in the car.
The clinician stated that needing the daughter's help counts as a severe hypo, and if another severe hypo occurs within 12 months or while driving, the patient must stop driving and tell the DVLA.
The clinician planned to refer the patient to the podiatrist for the callus and book his eye screening.
The clinician scheduled a review in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.

findings.transcript_evidence: I'd like to add a tablet called empagliflozin, 10 milligrams once a day.
findings.rationale: The note incorrectly documents the dose of empagliflozin as 100 mg, while the transcript confirms the prescribed dose is 10 mg.
